claims.claim: Cyril of Alexandria was bishop of Alexandria from 412 until his death in 444.
Cyril was born circa 375–376 and died in 444.
Cyril succeeded his uncle Theophilus as bishop of Alexandria in 412.

In 362/363 the Roman emperor Julian composed a treatise titled Against the Galileans in which he set forth his reasons for abandoning Christianity and returning to devotion to the traditional Greco-Roman deities.
Sixty years later Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, composed a response titled Against Julian.
The translators date Cyril's treatise to the mid-420s, based on parallels with his festal letters from that period.
Julian's treatise was the most sophisticated critique of Christianity to have been composed in antiquity.
Cyril's Against Julian would dwarf the size of Julian's original work.
Cyril's treatise serves as our primary source for the fragments of Julian's original work that have survived.
Cyril's rebuttal was equally learned and drew upon a wide range of ancient literature, including poetry, history, philosophy, and religious works.
The work probably originally comprised twenty books.
Only half of Cyril's work has survived intact, with Books I–X preserved; the latter ten books are lost and survive only in quotations in later Greek and Syriac sources.
